name: Iris Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer for health and personal-care products at Calder Pharmacy Wholesale. We supply about 900 independent pharmacies with things like vitamins, cold remedies, nappies and toothpaste. I start at half past six with my AI assistant, which reads the overnight stock levels and flags what's likely to run out. By nine I'm negotiating with the big brands' account managers, and the afternoon is spent on promotions and a long review with my four buyers. On Fridays I check the numbers by hand, just to keep my eye in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is helping a small pharmacist stay open. If I get her the right cold remedy at the right price in January, she survives the winter. What wears me out is the brands' tactics, which are relentless. My husband Viktor keeps the books for a family hardware shop, and he says I argue with the sales reps in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are practical. At work I'd say use them for what works, and stop pretending it's more. At church I'd say the Lord gave us work, and tools are tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm happy. The assistant already saves me about 8 hours a week, and I use the time to visit pharmacies, which is what actually wins business. I'm 58 and well paid, and I'd quite like a plain few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep improving the way I use the tools. I'd start training the junior buyers in how to ask good questions of the assistant. I'd also keep up with Viktor's savings plan for retirement at 63, and put a little more into the church building fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. No drama needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI is mostly hype, do you feel you've bet on the wrong horse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at all. I never bet on a promise. I use what saves time. If the hype fades, I have still saved my 8 hours, and I use them on people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your faith and your community tell you about change like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our faith says we are stewards, not owners. We use what we're given with care, and we help one another. I treat tools like that: use them well, do not worship them. My priest likes to say, a hammer is neither good nor evil.

say: I'd say the tools are **practical**, so use them for what works and stop pretending it's more.
At church I'd say tools are tools.
think: Privately I'm happy: the assistant saves me about **8 hours** a week for pharmacy visits.
I'd like a **plain** few years before retiring.
do: Keep improving my use of the assistant and train junior buyers to **ask good questions**.
Stick to Viktor's **retirement plan** for 63 and give a little more to the church building fund.
S0.quote: I never bet on a promise. I use what saves time.
fieldNote: Her **calm** is practical: she measures the tools by hours saved.
Faith frames tools as things to use with care, not to worship.
Time saved goes to pharmacy visits, which she says wins business.

steps.text: Train junior buyers to ask the assistant better questions
Spend the saved hours visiting independent pharmacies
Keep to Viktor's savings plan for retiring at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, and we have to do it with care. At work I'd say adopt it, but protect our people. At church I'd say love your neighbour: don't push anyone off a cliff for the sake of a margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the first thing that worries me. The assistant could do most of what my junior buyers do, and half of mine. Calder might reduce the buying team to two. I'd be one of them, because I'm senior and the assistant likes me, but the others wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose that Calder retrains the buyers into pharmacy advisers, who visit shops and help them plan. I'd automate routine buying fully this year, so we show what's possible. And I'd take a short course in supply-chain analytics, to stay ahead of what Calder will ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job is likely safe, but my people's are not, and I'd feel responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If buying is one of the first jobs software does, what do you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel and Lina. Pavel has a family, a small child and a mortgage. Lina's quick, and would find work easily. I'd fight hardest for Pavel (one of my buyers), not because I like him more, but because he has more to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you look after the four buyers in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The relationships with pharmacists, and the judgement on promotions and stock levels. I'd keep a human voice on the phone for a pharmacist who is worried about winter. The assistant is good, but it doesn't know that Mr Hadid's shop is in a student area, and the students buy cough sweets in a different way.

say: I'd say it's serious, so adopt it but **protect our people**.
At church I'd say love your neighbour and don't push anyone off a cliff for a margin.
think: Privately the assistant could do most of my juniors' work and half of mine, so the team may fall to **two**.
My job is likely safe, but I'd feel **responsible** for the others.
do: Propose that Calder retrains buyers as **pharmacy advisers**, and automate routine buying fully this year.
Take a short course in **supply-chain analytics** to stay ahead.
feel: **Uneasy**: my own job looks safe, but my people's don't.
S1.quote: I'd fight hardest for Pavel (one of my buyers), not because I like him more, but because he has more to lose.
fieldNote: Her **unease** is for others: Pavel and Lina, her buyers.
She will automate her own team's work, then fight to redeploy them.
Moral frame is explicit: love your neighbour.

steps.text: Propose retraining the buyers as pharmacy advisers
Automate routine buying fully this year
Take a short supply-chain analytics course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in a storm and we must hold together. At work I'd tell the truth. At church I'd ask for prayers and for practical help for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think both our jobs go. Mine because buying is thinking work, and Viktor's because bookkeeping is the sort of thing that goes first. Two incomes down at once, at 58, with the mortgage nearly paid but not quite. It's the thing that would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Viktor and set a hard budget. We'd pay off the mortgage with some of our savings, and put the rest where it's safe. I'd press Calder for a deal, and ask the church about its job help for older members. And I'd look at consulting for small pharmacies, using what I know, in case they'd pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the doubling that scares me. One of us losing a job is a bump. Both of us, in the same two years, is something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Viktor's work is bookkeeping. What does that mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia is a physiotherapist, so her work is hands-on, and safer. Anton is a software developer, and I think he'll be hit early. I'd tell them both: we're fine for money, but we'll not be able to help forever, so let's make a plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children, Nadia and Anton?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both of us would go back to basics. Viktor knows how to fix up a shop, and I could do a job in a pharmacy, though it wouldn't pay as well. We'd rather work in a humbler role than sit at home.

say: I'd say we're in a **storm** and must hold together, and I'd tell the team the truth.
At church I'd ask for prayers and practical help for families.
think: Privately both our jobs go: buying and **bookkeeping** are thinking work.
Both of us losing income in two years is what would keep me **awake**.
do: Set a hard **budget** with Viktor and pay off the mortgage with part of our savings.
Press Calder for a deal and offer **consulting** to small pharmacies.
feel: **Alarmed**: one lost job is a bump, but two in the same years is something else.
S2.quote: One of us losing a job is a bump. Both of us, in the same two years, is something else.
fieldNote: The **doubling** of exposure, buying plus bookkeeping, makes her alarmed despite savings.
Her humility surfaces: she would take humbler work rather than stay at home.
Worries about son Anton's coding career.

steps.text: Set a hard budget with Viktor and clear the mortgage
Offer consulting to small pharmacies who trust me
Ask the church about job help for older members
Work in a pharmacy or hardware shop if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us a chance, and we should not waste it. At work I'd start the transition now. At church I'd say prepare our children and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's better, but the same worry stays: Viktor's job and mine. I'd be 63, so I could stop. He's 60, and he could, too, with a smaller pension. It's a squeeze but not a drowning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start consulting for pharmacies on the side, one day a week, to see if it works. I'd train Pavel to take over the big brand relationships. And I'd ask Viktor to learn to do bookkeeping with the tools, and to offer his services to small shops that can't afford a big firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can work with it. I'd make a plan and tick it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the church to run a mentoring scheme, with older members like me teaching skills to younger ones. And a fund for families who are hit hard, run by the parish and not the state. It's what a community is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the church and community to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also want Anton to think about moving from pure coding to something that needs people, like helping pharmacies use the tools. He's resistant, but he's a good boy and will listen.

say: I'd say it gives us a **chance** and we should not waste it, so I'd start the transition now.
At church I'd say prepare our children and help each other.
think: Privately the worry stays: **Viktor's job and mine**, though at 63 and 60 we could stop.
It's a squeeze but not a drowning.
do: Start **consulting** for pharmacies one day a week and train Pavel to take over the brand relationships.
Ask Viktor to offer **tool-assisted bookkeeping** to small shops.
feel: **Anxious**, but workable: I'd make a plan and tick it off.
S3.quote: I'd want the church to run a mentoring scheme, with older members like me teaching skills to younger ones.
fieldNote: Five years let her turn **worry into a plan** with ticks.
Wants community, not the state, to carry hardship.
Hopes Anton will move toward work that needs people.

steps.text: Start consulting for pharmacies one day a week
Train Pavel to take over the big brand relationships
Ask Viktor to offer tool-assisted bookkeeping to small shops
Help set up a parish mentoring scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's plenty of time, and we should build the right things. At work I'd keep leading the way on the tools. At church I'd say train the young and look after the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm calm. I'd be retired and Viktor too. I'd be glad if things went well, and sad if my children's world was harder than ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 63, then do a few days a month of paid advice. I'd keep putting money into a world fund and into the church's building. And I'd help Nadia buy a physio clinic, if she wants one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off, and I'd have time to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you well into retirement. What do you want from that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia running a clinic with her own name on the door. Anton doing something thoughtful and not just coding, maybe teaching. And grandchildren, if God is willing, who learn to use the tools and also to wait their turn and say thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope your children will be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I did the best I could with what I'd been given. That's the thing I'd like said.

say: I'd say it's plenty of time, so build the **right things** and keep leading on the tools.
At church I'd say train the young and look after the old.
think: Privately I'm calm: I'd be **retired**, and glad if things go well.
I'd be sad only if my children's world were harder than ours.
do: Work until **63**, then do a few paid advice days a month.
Keep investing in a world fund and help Nadia buy a **physio clinic**.
feel: **Calm**: it's a long way off, and there's time to do things.
S4.quote: I did the best I could with what I'd been given. That's the thing I'd like said.
fieldNote: Distance brings **calm** and a legacy mindset.
Savings go toward her daughter's clinic.
Humble in tone, with faith in the background, and keen that her children find work with people in it.

steps.text: Work until 63 then do a few paid advice days a month
Help Nadia buy a physiotherapy clinic
Keep investing in a world fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because Viktor's job and mine would both go with no time to adjust. What would help is early warning from employers, a fund for retraining that firms pay into, and communities that step in. I'm happy to adapt, but I need time and a fair start for those who can't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only this. Being adaptive isn't the same as being unafraid. I'd like us all to get through it, not just the quick ones. I'm quick with the tools, but I have a husband, children and people I buy for.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive isn't the same as being unafraid. I'd like us all to get through it, not just the quick ones.
portrait: Iris is a **58-year-old** senior buyer of health and personal-care products for a pharmacy wholesaler, and uses AI tools every day.
She is a traditional, church-going free-marketeer who measures tools by hours saved and thinks of herself as a steward.
Her mood runs from calm to **alarmed** in the two-year world, because her husband's bookkeeping is also thinking work.
She blames no one, but wants firms to give early warning, and communities and churches to catch those who fall.
Savings, a daily AI habit and a **consulting** idea give her options; she fights hardest for her junior buyers.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, with her job and her husband's both going and no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** from employers, a firm-funded retraining fund and communities that step in for those who can't adapt.
